content: It is primarily used to describe rotational speed or angular velocity. While the symbol r/min is recommended by standards organizations for consistency with other unit symbols, alternative abbreviations like rpm or RPM are widely used. In French, for instance, tr/mn (tours par minute) is common. Angular velocity in SI is often expressed in radians per second (rad/s). To convert rpm to hertz, divide the rpm value by 60. Here are specific examples of rpm usage in various contexts: 1. Recording Media: The rotational speed of disc or tape-based recording media is often specified in rpm. For example, gramophone records typically rotate at 16, 33⅓, 45, or 78 rpm, corresponding to approximately ⁴⁄₁₅, ⁵⁄₉, ³⁄₄, or 1.3 Hz. 2. Dental Drills: Modern dental drills can achieve rotational speeds of up to 500,000 rpm, equivalent to 8 kHz. 3. Clock Mechanisms: The second hand of a traditional analog clock completes one full rotation per minute, or 1 rpm. 4. Audio CD Players: Audio CD players maintain a constant data read rate of 150 kB/s. To achieve this, the disc's rotational speed varies from approximately 500 rpm (8 Hz) at the innermost edge to 200 rpm (3.5 Hz) at the outer edge. CD-ROM drives are rated in multiples of this base speed, though they do not maintain a constant read rate for most disc formats. 5. DVD Players: DVD players also operate at a constant linear read rate. The disc's rotational speed ranges from 1,530 rpm (25.5 Hz) at the innermost edge to 630 rpm (10.5 Hz) at the outer edge. DVD drive speeds are typically expressed as multiples of this base rate. 6. Washing Machines: During spin cycles, the drum of a washing machine may rotate at speeds between 500 and 2,000 rpm, corresponding to 8–33 Hz. 7. Automobile Engines: The rotational speed of a car engine typically ranges from 700 to 7,000 rpm (12–120 Hz), though high-performance engines can reach up to 11,000 rpm (180 Hz). 8. Piston Aircraft Engines: These engines generally operate at speeds between 2,000 and 3,000 rpm, equivalent to 30–50 Hz. 9. Computer Hard Drives: Standard hard drives with ATA or SATA interfaces commonly rotate at 5,400 or 7,200 rpm (90 or 120 Hz). High-performance drives, often using SATA, SCSI, or Fibre Channel interfaces, can achieve speeds of 10,000 or 15,000 rpm (160 or 250 Hz). 10. Formula One Engines: The engines of Formula One racing cars can reach rotational speeds of up to 19,000 rpm (320 Hz) under certain conditions. 11. Uranium Enrichment Centrifuges: Zippe-type centrifuges used for uranium enrichment can spin at speeds of 90,000 rpm (1,500 Hz) or higher. 12. Gas Turbine Engines: These engines operate at extremely high rotational speeds, often in the tens of thousands of rpm. For example, JetCat model aircraft turbines can exceed 100,000 rpm (1,700 Hz), with some reaching up to 165,000 rpm (2,750 Hz). 13. Electromechanical Batteries (EMBs): EMBs, which use magnetically levitated flywheels in a vacuum, typically operate in the range of 60,000–200,000 rpm (1–3 kHz). The flywheel material is chosen not for its density but for its ability to safely disintegrate at surface speeds approximately seven times the speed of sound. 14. Turbochargers: Turbochargers can achieve rotational speeds of up to 290,000 rpm (4,800 Hz), with typical operating ranges between 80,000 and 200,000 rpm (1–3 kHz).
